data.title: Go Bicycling
data.shortDescription: Bicycle—including ebikes—use is permitted on paved park roads and parking areas open to the public as well as some areas listed in the main text. Be careful along park roads—everyone is looking at the view!

images.altText: Two people on a yellow and red tandem bike ride past blue striped badlands.
images.title: Pedal the Petrified Tandem Bike
images.caption: Pedal through the Petrified riders at Blue Mesa

data.activityDescription: Bicycles are allowed along the park road, but not along the trails except for a short access trail at Long Logs/Agate House trails. The routes are old highways or roads that are not maintained except for the eastern section of Route 66 that is graveled.
data.locationDescription:
Old 180 East

0.5 access trail to Long Logs and Agate House trails

Petroglyph Canyon

Route 66 East
data.longDescription:
There are several routes in the park that you can ride a bike. There are also bike racks scattered at overlooks and parking lots throughout the park.

36 CFR §4.30 – BICYCLES

(a) Bicycle/e-bike use is permitted on paved park roads and parking areas open to the public.

The following routes are closed to bicycle/e-bike use: Paved trails and all park lands not covered by pavement, with the exception of:

the unpaved portion of Old Route 66 from the main park road to the east boundary fence

the eastern portion of Old Highway 180 in the Rainbow Forest area from its intersection with the main park road to the east boundary

the portion of the Long logs trail from its intersection with the main park road, continuing to the trailhead loop area approximately ½ mile up the trail.

the trail beginning at the Rainbow Forest Picnic Area, and continuing to the base of the mesa, ending at a loop in the road (approximately 1 mile in length).

(b) The term “e-bike” means a two- or three-wheeled cycle with fully operable pedals and an electric motor of less than 750 watts (1 h.p.).

E-bikes are allowed in Petrified Forest National Park where traditional bicycles are allowed. E-bikes are prohibited where traditional bicycles are prohibited. Except where use of motor vehicles by the public is allowed, using the electric motor to move an e-bike without pedaling is prohibited.

A person operating an e-bike is subject to the following sections of 36 CFR part 4 that apply to the use of traditional bicycles: sections 4.12, 4.13, 4.20, 4.21, 4.22, 4.23, and 4.30(h)(2)-(5).

Except as specified in this Compendium, the use of an e-bike within Petrified Forest National Park is governed by State law, which is adopted and made a part of this Compendium. Any violation of State law adopted by this paragraph is prohibited.

data.title: Collect Your Cancellation Stamps

images.altText: Woman inside stamping in booklet on counter, displays in background.
images.title: Stamping Passport
images.caption: Collecting Cancellation Stamp

data.accessibilityInformation: Visitor Centers are accessible for mobility devices with push button doors.
data.ageDescription: We've seen all ages work on their stamp collection.
data.petsDescription: Only service animals allowed inside the buildings.
data.activityDescription: Collect your cancellation stamp from one the visitor centers. The cancellation ink usually reflects the color section of the passport—e.g. Petrified Forest has green ink for the green section. There are multiple dated stamps as well as a couple of image stamps.
data.longDescription: Collect your cancellation stamp! Collecting cancellation stamps has been popular for many visitors for decades, one of the first things they ask for when they enter the visitor centers. The cancellation ink usually reflects the color section of the passport—e.g. Petrified Forest has green ink for the green section. There are multiple dated stamps as well as a couple of image stamps. People use the passports, journals, postcards, brochures, maps, and other creative places.

data.title: Walk Long Logs Trail
data.shortDescription: Explore this ancient log jam at the base of purple and gray badlands along a paved half-mile loop.

images.altText: Late light on gray and purple badlands behind petrified logs under a lavender sky
images.title: Walk Long Logs Trail
images.caption: Long Logs Trail

data.location: Long Logs Trail, Petrified Forest National Park
data.accessibilityInformation:
The first half-mile of this trail is paved and suitable for mobility equipment and strollers. Strollers may be negotiated on the loop, but it is not recommended for most wheelchairs and other mobility equipment due to its narrow turns, grade, and rough surface.

Tread width: 85 in (216 cm), min 50 in
Grade: 3.5%, max 20.5%
Cross Slope: 2.9%, max 17.4%
data.petsDescription:
BARK Ranger:
·Bag your pet’s poop.
·Always keep your pet on a leash.
·Respect wildlife.
·Know where you can go.
data.activityDescription: Round trip, Long Logs Trail is a relatively easy walk of 1.6 miles along a paved path. There are many long petrified logs and a lot of petrified wood pieces near scenic gray and purple badlands.
data.locationDescription: Park at Rainbow Forest, walk across the bridge, continue up the 1/2 mile access trail, stay twards the left for the 1/2 mile Long Logs Loop.
data.longDescription: Long Logs is one of the largest concentrations of colorful petrified wood in the park, including some of the longest logs. Explore this ancient log jam at the base of purple and gray badlands along a paved half-mile loop (access trail is 0.5-mile one way—you can add this with Agate House Trail). Please leave petrified wood for others to enjoy. Report any removal of petrified wood or other materials to park staff.
data.durationDescription: Depends of the individual's interest and ability.

data.title: Walk the Tawa Trail
data.shortDescription: Enjoy the tranquility of the grassland as the paved trail leads you to scenic Tawa Point. The 1.2-mile one way Tawa Trail is a perfect place to stretch your legs after a long road trip.

images.altText: Man walking a trail under a sunset sky with clouds
images.title: Tawa Trail
images.caption: Walking the Tawa Trail

data.location: Tawa Trail Trailhead, Petrified Forest National Park
data.accessibilityInformation:
Hard-surface, wide trail, plenty of places to turn around as needed. 

Meets standards for outdoor developed areas.

Typical grade 2.3% with grades up to 8.3%
Typical Cross Slope: 2%                                 
Max Cross Slope: 5%
Typical Tread Width: 60 in (152.4 cm)
No obstacles
data.petsDescription:
BARK Ranger:
·Bag your pet’s poop.
·Always keep your pet on a leash.
·Respect wildlife.
·Know where you can go.
data.activityDescription: You can start the 1.2-mile one way walk from either the Painted Desert Community Complex or Tawa Point. There is a bench along the way to sit and enjoy the view. It is a relatively easy, hard-surfaced, path through the grassland.
data.locationDescription: The south trailhead for Tawa trail is located near the entrance station at the Painted Desert Community Complex.
data.longDescription: Enjoy the tranquility of the grassland as the paved trail leads you to scenic Tawa Point. The 1.2-mile one way Tawa Trail is a perfect place to stretch your legs after a long road trip. You will have views of the shortgrass prairie (particularly nice during wildflower season) and the red part of the Painted Desert. In Hopi ideology, Tawa refers to the Sun Spirit, the creator of the World. The Hopi are one of several modern Native American groups who are connected to the rich, varied history of Petrified Forest.

data.title: Enjoy Horseback Riding
data.shortDescription: Bring your own horse and take a ride into the backcountry.

images.altText: More than three horses and riders going down a trail into the red part of the Painted Desert, red ba
images.title: Horse Around
images.caption: Horses and riders heading down into the north unit of the wilderness area

data.accessibilityInformation: Up to the individual's knowledge and abilities.
data.petsDescription: Animals are allowed in the park as long as they are under control with leash, tether, or reins. Clean up their droppings. Use weed free feed. Respect wildlife and don't share food or approach. Know where you can go.
data.activityDescription: Bring your own mount and bring them into the park for riding in the backcountry. You will need water, weed free feed, clean up, and enjoy! Horses aren't allowed along the paved trails and roads, except for the wilderness access trail. You can also bring llamas, burros, whatever!
data.longDescription: Horse around! Bring your own horse and take a ride into the backcountry. While horses aren’t allowed on most of the trails, they can be ridden into the backcountry including the wilderness area. Be sure to clean up, use weed free feed, and bring all your water. A great place to start is the large parking lot at Kachina Point where you can find the access trail into the north unit of the wilderness area.

data.activityDescription: Walk a 1-mile round trip dirt trail with drop offs and spectacular views of the red part of the Painted Desert.

Below, the view features red badlands and crenulated white tuff.

data.accessibilityInformation: Suitable for strollers and various mobility equipment (power and manual), except on short trail spurDepending on the individual, most of this trail is accessible for mobility devices. The surface is hard, paved or graveled. Exhibits have proper contrast for visibility challenges.
data.petsDescription:
BARK Ranger:
·Bag your pet’s poop.
·Always keep your pet on a leash.
·Respect wildlife.
·Know where you can go.
data.activityDescription: Easy paved loop through an archeological site with wayside exhibits.
data.locationDescription: The Puerco Pueblo Trail starts at the parking lot near mile marker 11.
data.longDescription: The 3/4 -mile paved Puerco Pueblo Trail features the remnants of a hundred room masonry pueblo, occupied by the ancestral Puebloan people over 600 years ago. Petroglyphs can be viewed along the south end of the trail, including one that interacts with the rising sun on the summer solstice. Please do not climb on the boulders or walls and do not touch the petroglyphs. There is a mini museum halfway along the trail with cultural, archeological, and historical exhibits inside a CCC-built structure.

data.title: Walk Blue Mesa Trail
data.shortDescription: This 1-mile alternately paved and gravel trail loop offers the unique experience of hiking among banded badland hills of bentonite clay as well as petrified wood.

images.altText: Two hikers walk amidst gray, blue, and purple badlands along a trail
images.title: A Couple Walking Blue Mesa Trail
images.caption: A Couple Walking Blue Mesa Trail

data.location: Blue Mesa Trail, Petrified Forest National Park
data.seasonDescription: There can be ice in the winter.
data.accessibilityInformation: Most of this trail is not accessible for mobility devices. Steep grade near beginning of trail. The surface is hard, paved or graveled. Exhibits have proper contrast for visibility challenges.
data.petsDescription:
BARK Ranger:
·Bag your pet’s poop.
·Always keep your pet on a leash.
·Respect wildlife.
·Know where you can go.
data.activityDescription: This is a 1-mile paved/graveled trail with a steep section. There are wayside exhibits along the pathway. There is a bench at the trailhead under the sunshelter.
data.locationDescription: The Blue Mesa trailhead is located halfway around the Blue Mesa Road loop, next to a sun shelter.
data.longDescription: Steeply descending from the mesa top, this 1-mile alternately paved and gravel trail loop offers the unique experience of hiking among blue, purple, peach, and gray banded badland hills of bentonite clay as well as petrified wood. Numerous plant and animal fossils have been found by paleontologists in the sedimentary layers of Blue Mesa.
data.durationDescription: The trail is a mile, most of it is relatively easy, with one short steep section. Depends on the individual's speed walking and if you read the wayside exhibits or not.

data.petsDescription: Only service animals are allowed in the museum.

data.activityDescription: Fossils found in the park from the Late Triassic are featured in many displays in the Rainbow Forest Museum.

data.longDescription: Explore the paleontology exhibits at Rainbow Forest Museum. The exhibits will help understand the world of the Late Triassic, how petrified wood formed, and see fossils some of the animals and plants that once lived here.
data.durationDescription: Depends on your interest. The exhibits are visually interesting and there is a hierarchy of text for more information.

data.title: Watch Wildlife
data.shortDescription: Watching wildlife is a seasonal activity, but just in that the species to watch change, particularly in birdwatching.

images.altText: Small herd of tan and white pronghorn, hooved native animal, on grassland with late afternoon light.
images.title: American Pronghorn
images.caption: American Pronghorn are one of the native animals in the park

data.seasonDescription: Wildlife changes throughout the year, birds best in spring and fall.
data.accessibilityInformation: Most overlooks are accessible for mobility challenges with large paved spaces.
data.petsDescription: Just remember that a pet may hinder your ability to see wildlife. Be sure they are leashed.
data.timeOfDayDescription: At this time, there is no overnight camping in the park, so we are limited to park operating hours.
data.activityDescription: Bring your binoculars and telephoto lenses to view the wildlife of Petrified Forest National Park. There are many animals that live in the park, although a lot are nocturnal, but do give them room and respect. Watch from afar, don't approach, never feed (that includes ravens), and remember that they are wild. You can see deer in the grassland and mesas, pronghorn in the open prairie, elk near the river corridor, eagles between mile marker 8 and Puerco Pueblo, birds around the facilities and water sources, lizards along trails and anywhere they can sun themselves. Birds are best in spring and fall.
data.longDescription: Watching wildlife is a seasonal activity, but just in that the species to watch change, particularly in birdwatching. We are located along a fairly active branch of the north-south migratory pathways, so visitors in spring and fall get a treat. We can see many different types of songbirds, raptors, even waterfowl. You can also watch for pronghorn, coyotes, and ravens year-round. Please remember not to feed, harass, or get too close as these are wild critters!
data.durationDescription: Depending on your interest, you can look for animals when you stop at an overlook or you can spend hours looking for birds in the cottonwoods.

data.title: Take a Self-Guided Tour of Giant Logs
data.shortDescription: Take a self-guided tour of Giant Logs, one of the highest concentration of large, colorful petrified logs.

images.altText: Many people walking along a trail under cloudy skies, surrounded by chunks of petrified wood.
images.title: Visitors on Giant Logs Trail
images.caption: Visitors on Giant Logs Trail

data.location: Giant Logs Trail, Petrified Forest National Park
data.accessibilityInformation:
Hard paved or graveled surface
Tread width: 57 in (145.6 cm), min 48 in (121.9 cm)
Grade: 4.8%, max 19.1%
Cross Slope: 2.5%, max 13.4%

Booklet with text has good constrast.
Audio is not available.
data.activityDescription: Get the self-guiding booklet from the museum/visitor center. Walk the butterfly-shaped trail behind the museum. Numbers on posts go with the booklet description.
data.locationDescription: The trailhead for Giant Logs Trail is behind the Rainbow Forest Museum at the south end of Petrified Forest National Park, mile marker 26.
data.longDescription: Take a self-guided tour of Giant Logs, one of the highest concentration of large, colorful petrified logs. The trail is shaped like a butterfly, the “head” is Old Faithful, the most massive log in the park. The trail has a hard surface, partially paved and graveled. There are posts with numbers that go along with the self-guiding tour booklet available at the Rainbow Forest Museum. The trail is 0.4 miles round trip, about 30 minutes long, rated easy.
data.durationDescription: Depends so much on the individual, but most people need at least 30 minutes and most finish within an hour.
